title: The Survey
summary: The film becomes the market seen from straight above: a night survey of a city grid, with traffic moving in every direction and a fast expressway along the river. On top of it, Kelwin's own route is drawn in one crisp line that picks up three systems on three blocks and drops toward the button, so the video is the ground the drawing reads, not decoration behind a headline.

reference.borrowed: Runway: a slow aerial as an enterprise hero, where terrain reads as scale and seriousness rather than lifestyle. Cohere (refs/hero-r6-15.webp): a crisp instrument sitting on soft aerial footage, where the contrast of soft ground and sharp tool is the message. Neon (refs/hero-r6-7.webp): footage that is itself data (light), behind a left-aligned headline, so the video reads as infrastructure.
reference.kelwin: The aerial is shot straight down (no horizon, no perspective), graded graphite with warm sand lights and no neon, and seen through the same frost and grain as today's film. The tool is not a product screenshot. It is one 1px route in the same drawing language as the approved sections: square nodes, the 01/02/03 code boxes from the System and Reframe callouts, and right-angle turns only. The type keeps hero U's exact positions.

video: What the mockup uses: no new footage and no photograph. The film is drawn live on a <canvas> inside .km-film, in place of today's plate. It shows a night city from directly above. The streets are graded like a real one: two lit avenues, busy streets and quiet ones, and block widths that vary. There are dark roofs with sparse rooftop lights, a riverside expressway along the waterfront in the lower left, and a dark park under the lede and the buttons, so they sit on calm ground. Car lights travel along every street in both directions. The expressway carries the densest, fastest traffic (about 40px a second), which is what makes the frame read as footage at a glance. A boat crosses the river, two cloud shadows drift over in 40 seconds, and the camera sways about 14px either side of rest over a 40-second cycle as a pure sideways move. Kelwin's route rides exactly the same offset, so it stays pinned to its streets. The city is built once from the page's colour tokens, so both skins grade it. It is blurred and graded once (crushed blacks, so the lamps carry the frame rather than a haze), and each frame only blits that plate and the moving lights, at half resolution and 24 frames per second. That costs about 2% of one core for script, and it stops completely when the hero is off screen. There are no cuts, so the loop never jumps. Reduced motion shows one still frame. How the real film would be made: licensed 4K nadir (straight-down) drone or helicopter footage of a dense, orthogonal city grid at night, with a river expressway in frame, unidentifiable after grading. It would be 40 seconds of pure sideways pan with no rotation or zoom, graded to graphite blacks with warm sand lights and no neon, and delivered as one muted, seamless loop (H.265 MP4 + VP9 WebM, playsinline) with a poster frame. The alternative is a rendered orthographic flyover of a procedural city with instanced traffic (Blender or Houdini), exported as a seamless 30-second loop together with the per-frame camera offset. Either way the route reads that offset, or shares the video's CSS move, so it never slides off its streets.
motion: entrance (about 3s): the film fades up while the lens finds focus. The nav hairline draws and its two marks register, and the label, the statement and the red rule land with the kit's usual choreography. At 0.7s the three nodes appear as empty squares. At 0.9s the dashed raw signal runs in from the left edge along the avenue. At 1.6s the line turns solid at node 01 and the node latches (fills), and 'Narrative Systems' fades in. The line reaches node 02 at 1.9s and turns down the col-12 street to node 03 at 2.3s, latching each node and fading in its name as it arrives. The open chevron seats above the lede at about 2.8s. The lede, the audit note and the doors arrive with the head.

ambient: the footage runs continuously: traffic on every street, a fast stream on the riverside expressway, the boat, the cloud shadows and the slow camera sway. On top, one short bright pulse laps the solid route at constant speed (12 seconds a lap, linear), turning at the corner. That is the only drawn loop: one steady signal against a city moving every which way, which is the lede's 'fragmented growth into repeatable pipeline' made visible.
interaction: the three names are links to their Capabilities sections. Hovering or focusing one holds its stretch of the route at full white and dims the rest of the route.
off screen: the footage, the pulse and the grain all stop when the hero leaves the viewport and carry on when it returns.
reduced motion: one still frame of the city, the route fully drawn, the three nodes latched and no pulse. There are no timers and no loops.
addressed: There is a video playing behind the whole hero, and it now shows something: the market seen from above at night, with traffic moving on every street and a fast expressway along the river. It reads as aerial footage from a defense or infrastructure company, not as a stock clip of people in a room.

The film has a job. Kelwin's route is drawn on its streets, picks up Narrative Systems, GTM Infrastructure and GTM Intelligence, and drops toward the button. The footage is the market, and the line is the system Kelwin installs on it.

The hero is now the same material as the sections you approved: its blacks sit on the page's own graphite rather than a grey haze, and its drawing is the same 1px line, square nodes, 01/02/03 code boxes and right-angle turns. It becomes the page's first instrument instead of its only picture.

Nothing else moves on the layout. The type sits exactly where it does today, and the statement and lede read more clearly than in today's hero. 'Request a System Audit' sits at 768–824px at 1440×900, and at 683–732px at 1280×800.
There is no Pause film button, no caption strip and no figure numbering. The only red is the two label squares, the rule and the primary button. The drawing itself has no red.
notes: Stage 1440×960: nav 0–96 · route avenue y 200 · label 276–292 · statement 302–588 (116px, two lines) · rule 602 · lede 646–736 (cols 8–12) · doors 768–824 · audit note 754–830 (cols 1–4). The route: dashed raw signal from x 0 to the col-8 line at y 200, then solid through node 01 (843, 200) to node 02 (1066, 200, col 10) and the corner at col 12 (1289, 200). It drops to node 03 (1289, 322) and on down to an open chevron at y 612, 34px above the lede. Line 2 ends at x 1238, so the vertical clears 'problem.' by 50px. The solid route sits on a flat 4px graphite casing, as map routes do, so the 1px line stays crisp where it crosses the lit avenue. The route's three streets (cols 8, 10, 12) and the col-6 avenue sit on the page's column lines, so at rest the junctions share the lede's and the primary's spine. The other streets are set 10–20px off the columns so the blocks vary in width. The cross streets run through the gaps above, between and below the two statement lines, so no lit street crosses a letter. Contrast was measured on live frames over the 40s camera cycle, in both skins: lede at least 9.0:1, statement at least 8.3:1 (2nd percentile), the light accent 'problem.' at least 6.9:1, nav at least 5.6:1, and the names at least 9.2:1 on their flat graphite tags. Gradients appear only inside .km-film (the legibility scrim, the lens falloff and the canvas light sprites). Registration marks: two, on the nav hairline. Film settings: blur 8px and the frosted-glass grain are unchanged. The frost layer runs at 45% opacity: at full strength its white mottle lifts a night plate's blacks from about 8 to about 36, which reads as fog rather than glass. At 45% the blacks settle on the page's graphite. Changes from the concept: (1) node 03 sits at y 322, not 392, because 392 would put a lit street through line 1 of the statement; 322 is the street just above it. (2) The 6px packet became a short 18×3px pulse riding the line, because in stills a 6px square read as a fourth node. (3) The three names sit on flat graphite tags (code box + name) instead of loose text, so they stay crisp over bright traffic; 03 gets a 13px leader like 01 and 02. (4) The camera sways about 14px each side of rest over 40s (about 2% in all) rather than panning one way, so the route returns to the column grid. The route rides the sway, so between rests it can sit up to 14px off the lede's edge; that is the honest price of being pinned to the footage. (5) The canvas runs at half resolution and 24fps rather than at devicePixelRatio, since an 8px-blurred plate carries no finer detail, and the crisp line is SVG at full resolution. (6) Added beyond the concept: a riverside expressway with piers, a park under the lede, a boat, sparse rooftop lights, graded street classes and two cloud shadows instead of one, so the plate reads as a city rather than graph paper. Traffic runs from about 10px/s on quiet streets to about 25px/s on the avenues and about 40px/s on the expressway, faster than the concept's 6–14px/s, so the motion is noticeable. Flag: like the concept says, this drops the people-at-work film, your original idea, on purpose, to show the most high-tech end of the range.
